title: Body, Prāṇa and the Energetics of Experience
reflection: Start from the ground: check your posture and your breath once an hour today, and let the body lead.

questions.q: What does Conversation 3.7 mean by one energy at many speeds?
o: Body, breath, emotion and thought are one living energy, prāṇa, at different speeds.
The body is slow and the mind is fast, and the two have nothing at all to do with each other.
Energy is made in the body and spent by the mind, until the supply has run out.
Each person has a fixed amount of energy, and spends it at whatever speed they like.
questions.e: Like a single keyboard, from the lowest, slowest notes to the highest and finest, the body is the bass end and the mind the treble. There is no lesser end, so working with the body engages the same energy that becomes thought and awareness.
questions.c: Body to mind is one keyboard of one energy

questions.q: A man calls body practice a warm-up before the real work. What does Conversation 3.7 say?
o: No end of the keyboard is lesser: the contemplative traditions begin with breath and body.
He is right, since the body is the lowest note and the least of all of the energies there are.
He is right, as long as the body practice is kept very short and gentle at the start of it.
He is wrong, since body practice entirely replaces the need for any work at all on the mind.
questions.e: Because it is one keyboard, working with the body engages the very same energy that becomes thought and awareness. The contemplative traditions begin with breath and body and never treat them as a mere warm-up.
questions.c: The body is not a warm-up but the entrance

questions.q: Which of the five energies is the one of letting go, in Conversation 3.7?
o: Apāna: the out-breath, releasing finished thoughts and spent feelings.
Prāṇa: the in-breath, taking in through the senses and receiving what arrives.
Samāna: digesting food into nourishment and experience into understanding.
Udāna: reaching up through speech, effort, aspiration and growth in life.
questions.e: Weak apāna is the mind that keeps running a finished event. Prāṇa takes in, samāna digests, udāna reaches up and vyāna circulates and connects. The breath is the lever for several at once.

questions.q: A woman keeps replaying an event that ended days ago. Which energy does Conversation 3.7 point to?
o: Apāna, letting go: finished thoughts and spent feelings are not being released.
Prāṇa, taking in: she is receiving too little through her senses to settle.
Udāna, reaching up: she lacks the aspiration to move on from what has passed.
Vyāna, circulating: her body is numb, so nothing can pass from one part to another.
questions.e: Weak apāna is the mind that keeps running a finished event. A longer out-breath is one handle for letting go.
questions.c: A mind replaying a finished event: apāna

questions.q: A man is told to just calm down, and cannot. Why does slow breathing work when that does not, in Conversation 3.7?
o: The mind is too quick to grab, but it follows the slow handle of the breath down.
The breath is a trick, so it fools the mind into being calm for a short while.
The mind obeys commands, but only when they are repeated slowly and many times.
The breath works on the body alone, so the mind is left to settle on its own.
questions.e: The quick, flickering mind falls into step with whatever slow rhythm the body provides, like a boat riding the sea’s swell. At about six breaths a minute, longer out than in, heart and breath synchronise and the mind settles. This is why breath-work comes before attention training.
questions.c: Take the slow handle and the mind follows it down

questions.q: “Collapsed, numb and heavy states are laziness, which a person could end by deciding to.”
questions.e: Tamas is not laziness but a system protecting itself from overwhelm. The three states of the vagus nerve map onto the guṇas: safe and open is sattva, mobilised and racing is rajas, collapsed and numb is tamas.
questions.c: The collapsed state is protection, not laziness

questions.q: A man’s heart is racing, his mind is jumping and he feels narrowed and urgent. Which state does Conversation 3.7 name?
o: Rajas: the mobilised state, with the gain up, the noise up and the mind jumping.
Sattva: the safe state, open, connected and flexible, so the racing is a good sign.
Tamas: the collapsed state, in which the system has gone numb and heavy.
None of the three, since a racing heart belongs to the body and not the mind.
questions.e: Mobilised, racing, narrowed and urgent is rajas. Helping the body into the safe, settled state is how sattva is cultivated, and the mind clears as a direct result.
questions.c: Racing and narrowed is the rajas state

questions.q: “Conditioning is stored in the muscles and breath as well as in memory, which is why a tone of voice can trigger terror.”
questions.e: That is why talking alone often cannot reach it, and why body-based work can. Much of the mental noise is physical: pain, tiredness, hunger and an over-alert system.
questions.c: Conditioning is stored in the body as well as in memory

questions.q: A woman is overwhelmed and things feel out of all proportion. Which step fits Conversation 3.7?
o: Shift the gain through the body: an upright spine and open chest cue safety, and posture helps.
Reason with the feeling until it shrinks, since the gain is set by thought alone.
Push through and ignore the body, since it is a distraction from the real work.
Wait for the feeling to pass, since the gain cannot be moved by anything she does.
questions.e: The gain, how blown-out-of-proportion things feel, is set by the body’s state and can be shifted by posture. The body is not a distraction from the inner work: it is the entrance to it.
questions.c: The body sets the gain, and posture can shift it

questions.q: A teacher wants to start a lesson with a wired class. Which idea from Conversation 3.7 helps?
o: Begin from the ground: a slow breath, longer out than in, and an open posture.
Begin with a long talk on calm, since an idea of calm is the quickest way to settle.
Begin with the loudest pupils, since they alone set the state of the whole class.
Begin at once with the work, since the body can be left to settle by itself.
questions.e: Slow the breath to about six a minute, longer out than in, and the mind settles. An upright spine and open chest cue safety. The body is the entrance to the inner work.
questions.c: Begin from the ground: breath and posture
